title: Endpoint Denial of Service: Application Exhaustion Flood
shortTitle: Endpoint Denial of Service: Application Exhaustion Flood
summary: Application exhaustion floods push on the most expensive features an application offers rather than on the platform beneath it. Every non trivial application contains operations whose cost is far higher than the cost of asking for them: generating a report, running a wide database query, reindexing a search, rendering a large image, converting a document, or computing a password hash. Repeated requests to those paths consume processor time, memory, database connections, or temporary storage, and because the requests are syntactically valid the traffic looks ordinary at the network layer. Impact can be reached with rate limits that would be harmless against cheap endpoints, which makes per endpoint accounting essential; defenders need to know the unit cost of each function and how often it is called. Signals include a small number of endpoints accounting for a large share of resource use, request durations that exceed the application's own service targets, thread or worker pools blocked on the same expensive task, rising garbage collection or memory pressure, database connection pool exhaustion, and repeated identical parameters submitted far faster than a person could type them. Distinguishing attack from legitimate load is about distribution and purpose: real users spread their effort across features and reach goals, while abuse concentrates on one costly path and repeats it. Mitigations include per user and per address limits on costly operations, task queues with bounded concurrency, caching, and predictable failure rather than unbounded queuing.

beginner.definition: An application exhaustion flood abuses the slowest and heaviest features of an application. The attacker calls those features again and again. The application spends all its power on that work and cannot serve anyone else.
beginner.whyItMatters: These requests are valid, so a firewall sees nothing wrong and lets them through. Very few requests can be enough if each one is expensive to process. The outage can look like an ordinary performance problem. So teams may search for a code fault instead of an attacker. Without per feature limits, one abusive user can stop everyone.
howItWorks: The attacker studies the application and finds features that use heavy resources.
Examples include report generation, wide database searches, or long file conversion jobs.
They send repeated requests to that one feature, often with large inputs.
Each request occupies processor time, memory, or one database connection at a time.
Workers are all busy on the same task, so other requests wait in a queue.
The application slows down, times out, or stops responding to real users.
beginner.example: Imagine a quiet library where one visitor asks the night clerk for every book on a subject. The clerk must fetch and check each one. The clerk is busy for hours with a single request. Other visitors wait at the desk with simple questions. Nothing was broken and no rule was broken, yet the library stopped helping people.
takeaways: This sub-technique attacks the application's own expensive features.
Valid looking requests mean network defences alone cannot stop it.
Limits and queues around costly operations are the practical fix.

objectives: Explain how application exhaustion differs from service exhaustion floods.
Describe how repeated costly feature requests exhaust shared resources.
Explain why valid requests pass network defences without alarm.
Identify per endpoint metrics that expose abuse of expensive features.
Distinguish genuine heavy use from deliberate concentration on one path.
Describe controls such as concurrency limits and caching for costly operations.
